segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say, "I don't want the door to close on me"? So, what was "to close"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: La puerta. Which is related to ports, of course. You stress down on the O of ports and you get puerto. Puerto is port, and you change the O to an A and you get puerta, door. So, "I don't want the door to close on me"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No quiero la puerta... Oh, I don't want that the door closes on me.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No quiero que la puerta se me cierre.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. After "quiero que", "no quiero que", we're using the mood tense. "No quiero que la puerta se me cierre", or "No quiero que se me cierre la puerta". Good. How do you say "again", or "another time"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "I don't want the door to close on me again"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No quiero que la puerta se me cierre otra vez.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "No quiero que la puerta se me cierre otra vez". What was the verb "to return" or "to come back" and it's related to revolve?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Volver, good. Volver. Instead of saying "otra vez", another way of saying "again" in Spanish is to use "volver". So, for example, "it closes again", we can say "vuelve a cerrarse", "it returns to close". Why do we have "a" here? "Vuelve a cerrarse"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Because it's a verb of movement.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say, "I don't want the door to close again" with "volver"? How would it be? So let's take it from the beginning. "I don't want that"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "No quiero que la puerta vuelva a cerrarse", or "No quiero que vuelva a cerrarse la puerta". So "volver a" can be used like "again" and it's very common in Spanish, you might hear it around. So if you say, "I don't want it to happen again", for "to happen" you can use "to pass". What was "to pass"? Or if you don't remember you can make a guess here.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pasar, or "occur", "ocurrir", you can use that as well for happen; "suceder", succession, "suceder"—all of these mean to happen. Pasar is probably easier and easier to remember. So, "I don't want it to happen again. I don't want it to return to happen"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No quiero que vuelva a pasar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "No quiero que vuelva a pasar." Good. So we saw that we have the mood tense with which we are switching the vowel. So we go from "vuelve" to "vuelva" to get the mood tense. Or we have "cerrar" and we go from "cierra" to "cierre" to get the mood tense. We only have mood tense in the present and in the past. It doesn't exist in the futures. It used to, and there are a couple of words left behind in fixed expressions that still have this form, but for all intents and purposes it doesn't exist anymore in Spanish, the future mood tense. We have the present, which we've practiced and have a very good hold on, and the past mood tense. Now, the past mood tense is very easy to build. We will always build it going from the "they" form of the point in the past. And now that I've mentioned the point in the past, I should also mention that the mood tense for the past is the same for the line and the point. There are not two different ones; it counts for both. And we build it going from the point in the past for "they". So, for example, if we take a verb like "to speak", "hablar", and "they spoke"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, hablaron. So that's the first step to find the mood tense for the past is to go to the "they" form for the point in the past, hablaron. So you find "hablaron" and you change that last O to an A, and what do you get?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablaran. And that is your mood tense for "they" in the past. Now from that, we can work backwards to find the I, he, she, it, you formal version. If we work backwards from hablaran, what would we do to work backwards from hablaran? What would we get rid of?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablara. And then we can make the you informal version?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And "we"? And the accent won't move.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Habláramos. Good, so that's your set. We can do the same now with "comer". What was "they ate", the point in the past?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comieron, good. So now give me the mood tense version of "they ate".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comieran, good. And "I ate, he, she, it, you formal ate"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comieras. So this is how we form our mood tense in the past. We want to go from the "they" form. So we use this pretty much in the same kind of situations that we use the present mood tense, just in the past, with a couple of situations that are specifically for past. So for example, where "quiero que" necessitates the mood tense in the present, "quería que", "I wanted that", will necessitate the mood tense in the past. What is "I wanted" using the line in the past?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So now you could say something like, "I wanted them to eat with us. I wanted that they ate with us", and that "they ate", of course, will be in the mood tense. "I wanted that they ate with us"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "Quería que comieran con nosotros." And as we said, point in the past, line in the past, when it comes to the mood tense, it's the same. "I was hoping that he would call me." "I was hoping"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...that he would call me. So "I was hoping that..." We don't say "would", we use the past mood tense again. "I was hoping that he called me".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "Esperaba que me llamara." So whilst in English we would say, "I was hoping that he would call me", in Spanish, "I was hoping that he called me" and we use the past mood tense: "Esperaba que me llamara." Good. What was "to need" or "to necessitate"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Necesitar. How would you say "we needed", using the line in the past, "we needed, we were needing"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "Necesitábamos." How would you say, "We needed to speak with him. We needed to speak with him"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So here we don't need the mood tense: "Necesitábamos hablar con él", "We needed to speak with him". But if you were to say, "We needed that he speak with us. We needed that he spoke with us", then this "that", this "que", is what most of the time in Spanish is alerting you that maybe you want to use the mood tense. So "we needed that he speak with us", how is that?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. "Necesitábamos que hablara con nosotros." Very good. What was "to return", and we said that we can also use this verb like "again"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Volver. So if I wanted to say "I called you again", I could just say "I returned to call you". It's got nothing to do with actually returning, uh? It's just a way of saying again. So what is "I returned", from "to return", from "volver"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So "I called you again", speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "Volví a llamarte", "to organize", "in order to organize"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So all together: "I called you again in order to organize", speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "Volví a llamarte para organizar." So if we have "para organizar", we don't need to worry about the mood tense, and we can sometimes adjust our sentence putting "to" forms so that we can avoid finding the mood tense. So you could say something like, "Volví a llamarte para organizar", "Volví a llamarte para organizar", "I called you again in order to organize", and there you don't need the mood tense. But if you were to say, "I called you again so that / in order that we organized", then there you would have to use the mood tense. So how would that be? "I called you again", informally still?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...we organized. So it's the mood tense now, in the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Very good. So you have to take a trip through, ah, to find it. And it's quite time consuming at the beginning, but once you start practicing this past mood tense, of course it becomes much quicker to find these different forms. "Volví a llamarte para que organizáramos." And like I said, you can even avoid the use of the mood tense just by saying, "Volví a llamarte para organizar" in a structure like this one, for example. So we're seeing that they are similar structures to the structures we practiced the mood tense in the present with, just in the past.
